## Week 2, Session 4 — GAMs with mgcv {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv}

<div class="callout callout-note">
**Inference labs** use the five-step template:
Hypothesis → Visualise → Assumptions → Conduct → Conclude.
</div>

### Learning objectives {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv-learning-objectives}

- Fit a generalised additive model with `mgcv::gam()` and a single
  smooth term.
- Read effective degrees of freedom as a data-driven measure of
  flexibility.
- Visualise a smooth with `gratia::draw()` and report its shape in
  plain language.

### Prerequisites {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv-prerequisites}

Linear and multiple regression.

### Background {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv-background}

Generalised additive models replace the linear term β·X in a regression
with a smooth function f(X) estimated from the data. The smooth is
regularised so that wiggliness is penalised; the penalty strength is
chosen by restricted maximum likelihood or generalised cross-validation.
The effective degrees of freedom (edf) of the smooth quantifies how
much of that flexibility was used: an edf near 1 means the smooth is
essentially a line; an edf of 5 means something meaningfully curved.

GAMs are particularly useful when the *shape* of the relationship is
the scientific question. They are also useful as diagnostics for
linear models, because plotting a smooth against a predictor can
reveal a curve that the linear term would miss.

The `mgcv` package is the reference implementation. `gratia` is a
newer graphics layer on top of `mgcv` that produces tidy, ggplot-based
plots of smooths, partial effects, and derivatives.

### Setup {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv-setup}

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(mgcv)
library(gratia)
library(broom)
set.seed(42)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

### 1. Hypothesis {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv-1-hypothesis}

Simulate a sine-wave-plus-noise relationship and ask whether a GAM
recovers it while a linear model misses it.

### 2. Visualise {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv-2-visualise}

```r
n <- 300
x <- runif(n, 0, 4 * pi)
y <- sin(x) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.4)
dat <- tibble(x, y)

ggplot(dat, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "y")
```

### 3. Assumptions {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv-3-assumptions}

GAMs assume independent observations and a correctly specified
response distribution. The smooth flexibility is chosen automatically;
the user chooses the basis and, if relevant, the upper limit on
flexibility via `k`.

```r
fit_lm  <- lm(y ~ x, data = dat)
fit_gam <- gam(y ~ s(x, bs = "cr", k = 20), data = dat, method = "REML")

plot(fit_gam, residuals = TRUE, pch = 1, shade = TRUE)
gam.check(fit_gam)
```

`gam.check` reports `k-index` and effective df — an indication of
whether `k` is large enough.

### 4. Conduct {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv-4-conduct}

```r
summary(fit_gam)
AIC(fit_lm, fit_gam)
```

```r
draw(fit_gam)
```

### 5. Concluding statement {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv-5-concluding-statement}

> A GAM with a single smooth of x captured the non-linear relationship
> (edf = `round(summary(fit_gam)$s.table[,"edf"], 1)`; approximate
> *p* < 0.001). A linear model gave a near-zero slope because the
> underlying function is a full sine wave. The GAM is preferred when
> the shape, not a scalar slope, is the scientific object.


### Common pitfalls {#sec-chapters-07-regression-labs-lab-gams-with-mgcv-common-pitfalls}

- Setting `k` too small and constraining the smooth.
- Comparing GAMs with AIC as if it were a likelihood-ratio test.
- Reporting only the smooth without showing its plot.
